objective: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to write a descriptive profile of someone they know well, using compound sentences, adverbs of degree, and a clear PET article structure.
pet_task_prompt:
Question 2
You see this notice on your school website:

Articles wanted!
DESCRIBE SOMEONE YOU KNOW

Write an article about someone you know well.
What do they look like?
What are they like as a person?
What do they enjoy doing?

We'll publish the most interesting articles on our website.

Write your article in about 100 words.
materials:
- OFD2 pp.12-13
- Nureyev portrait (webp converted to jpg)
- Slide-deck: compound sentence review (7 questions), Nureyev portrait, PET article structure and useful language

stages.stage: Review — Compound Sentences and Sentence Errors
stages.stage_aim: To activate learners' prior knowledge of compound sentence structure and error correction in preparation for the writing task
stages.procedure: - Quick slide-based review: teacher displays 7 sentences — some correct, others containing fragments, run-ons, or comma splices. Students identify the error (or confirm the sentence is correct) and suggest a fix in open class. Teacher provides immediate feedback on each item. Bridge: 'These are the three checks you need before submitting any piece of writing — let's make sure today's profiles are error-free.'

stages.stage_aim: To spark interest in describing people and draw out descriptive vocabulary for appearance, personality, and interests
stages.procedure: - Display the Nureyev portrait on screen. Ask: 'What can you tell me about this person?' Elicit observations across four categories: personality, appearance, interests, and clothes/family. Students share ideas in open class. Teacher boards key vocabulary that emerges. Bridge: 'Just as we described Nureyev from a single portrait, you're going to describe someone you know inside and out.'

stages.stage: Preparation — Mind Map and Adverbs of Degree
stages.stage_aim: To generate and organise ideas for the writing task and practise using adverbs of degree for precise, accurate description
stages.procedure: - Students decide who they will write about. They complete the mind map (Exercise 3, p.12), identifying main categories — appearance, personality, interests — and adding specific details to each branch. Students then complete the adverbs of degree table (Exercise 5, p.13), classifying quite, a little, fairly, pretty, and really by intensity (small / medium / large degree). Quick whole-class check of answers.

stages.stage: PET Task Introduction — Article Structure and Useful Language
stages.stage_aim: To familiarise learners with the B1 Preliminary Writing Part 2 article format and equip them with a transferable structure, linking phrases, and descriptive language for the CA writing task
stages.procedure:
- Display the PET for Schools Writing Part 2 article prompt on screen. Walk through the four-part structure that examiners reward: (1) Catchy title — a short, interesting heading that tells the reader what the article is about. (2) Engaging opening — start with a question to hook the reader (Have you ever thought about who your favourite person is? / Let me tell you about someone very special.) or a bold personal statement. (3) Body — one paragraph per question from the prompt (appearance, personality, interests), using adverbs of degree for precision. (4) Closing — end with a question to the reader (What about you? Who do you admire?) or a final thought that wraps up the article.
- Show a reference slide with linking phrases grouped by function: opening (first of all, to begin with, let me tell you about...), adding ideas (also, what is more, on top of that, as well as this), contrasting (however, although), giving reasons (because, the reason is...), giving opinions (in my opinion, from my point of view, I think that...), and closing (all in all, to sum up).
- Show a second reference slide with useful phrases for describing people: He/She comes across as..., You can tell that..., What stands out most about him/her is..., One thing I have always noticed is..., He/She is the kind of person who...
- Students copy the four-part structure, linking phrases, and descriptive language frames into their notebooks for use during the writing stage.

stages.stage_aim: To produce a first draft of a descriptive profile that applies the mind map content, adverbs of degree, and the four-part PET article structure with linking language
stages.procedure: - Students write their first draft of the profile (about 100 words) using their mind map from Exercise 3 and the PET article scaffold from their notes. Requirements displayed on screen: (1) a catchy title, (2) an engaging opening, (3) one paragraph for each category — appearance, personality, interests — using at least three adverbs of degree from Exercise 5, (4) a closing question or final thought, (5) at least one compound sentence, and (6) at least two linking phrases from the reference slide. Remind students to check for run-ons, comma splices, and fragments as they write. Teacher circulates, offering individual support and noting common patterns for the next lesson.

stages.stage_aim: To reflect on the writing process and preview the peer-editing stage for next lesson
stages.procedure: - Quick show of hands: 'Who used at least two adverbs of degree?' 'Who wrote at least one compound sentence?' 'Who checked for run-ons and comma splices?' Celebrate wins. Preview: 'Next lesson we will do peer editing — swap profiles and check each other's work using the checklist from Exercise 7. Keep your draft safe.'
